title: POC — conversation shape & scaling forecast (Avalon Edge)
next_steps: Alex to share benchmark matrix and sample harness by 2026-09-27
Priya to schedule test window for 10k-chat replay by 2026-10-02
Avalon to provide 72h traffic logs and sample prompts by 2026-09-30
action_items: Alex Reed: send initial benchmark plan + load script template by 2026-09-27
Priya Nair: propose instance sizing (dedicated vs hosted variants) and quantization profile by 2026-09-29

summary: Kickoff scoping for a POC to validate conversation-driven inference for Avalon Edge. Main objectives: establish success criteria (p99 latency < 350ms for short turns, 95% of requests < 1s for medium turns), define workload shape (QPS bursts, steady-state concurrency), specify token input/output distributions and benchmarks, and align timelines for a 3-week pilot run. Security and deployment constraints discussed (VPC, KMS, audit logs). Next: Redwood to provide benchmark plan and instance sizing; Avalon to share traffic dumps and sample prompts.
topics: Workload characterization, QPS and burst modeling, concurrency and tail latency, token-length distribution, benchmark plan, success criteria, deployment modes (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private), security/KMS, test dataset and replay cadence, timeline and gating criteria.
transcript:
Header:
- Date/Time: 2026-09-23 16:00 UTC
- Duration: 47 minutes
- Recording: Zoom (auto-transcript)
- Attendees: Alex Reed (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood Solutions Eng), Samir Patel (Avalon Eng Lead), Maya Chen (Avalon SRE), Liam O'Connor (Avalon Product), Nina Alvarez (Avalon Security)

[00:00] Alex Reed: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call - alex here, ae for redwood inference, and joining me is priya and jordan from our eng team. samir, maya — want to kick us off with a sentence on what you hope to get out of today's call?

[00:18] Samir Patel: yeah uh sure, thanks alex. so we're scoping a POC to prove we can run our customer-facing chat workflows with consistent p99 latency and predictable costs. we want to validate both short-turn and multi-turn scenarios, see what the scaling profile looks like when we have bursts from campaigns, and make sure any private / vpc constraints are met.

[00:36] Maya Chen: and from ops perspective we need auditability and KMS integration, plus we want to stress tail latency under concurrency - we've seen tails kill UX in past pilots.

[00:49] Alex Reed: perfect — that's aligned. quick overview: typical POC flow we use is capture traffic, synthetic replay to reproduce QPS and token distribution, run bench with redwood hosted and a dedicated config, then analyze cost/latency/quality. priya will walk through the benchmark matrix and the telemetry we need.

[01:10] Priya Nair: cool. so i'm gonna share the two example workload sketches we use. (screen shuffle noise) um check if you can see my doc?

[01:22] Liam O'Connor: yep looks visible.

[01:25] Priya Nair: great. first is "conversational echo" - we saw ~70% of turns are short (input tokens under 30, latency-sensitive), 25% medium (30-150 tokens), and ~5% long (>150 tokens) mostly for summary or codegen. second is "session burst" - where a campaign causes a 5–8x QPS spike for 10–30 minutes with a raised fraction of medium-length turns. for sizing we need: expected steady QPS, expected burst multiplier, average and 95th token lengths for input+output, and concurrency target for 99th percentile latency.

[02:05] Samir Patel: for Avalon — current production baseline (we proxy through an older LLM endpoint) is around 12 QPS steady early morning, ramps to 110 QPS at peak with the marketing campaign. bursts historically hit ~420 QPS for ~20 minutes during big promo pushes. our average input tokens are 22, average output 46, but we do have long sessions where one response can be 400+ tokens (rare). our concurrency model is 3–4 requests per user session.

[02:36] Priya Nair: nice, that's really helpful. are those peaks single-region? or global?

[02:41] Samir Patel: primarily US-east with failover to EU-west for disaster, we haven't characterized cross-region routing for the POC.

[02:50] Jordan Lee: quick clarifying q — when you say 420 QPS burst, is that across all endpoints or just the chat generation path?

[02:56] Samir Patel: just chat generation. other endpoints are much lighter.

[03:02] Priya Nair: ok. so for the POC we'll focus on the chat generation flow. recommended bench plan: replay 72-hour representative trace compressed into a 6-hour test window to stress diurnal patterns, plus a focused 30-minute blast replicating the 420 QPS burst with token-mix matching your logs. we'll run both hosted-api and dedicated configs to compare latency and cost.

[03:26] Maya Chen: about the trace — we can sanitize logs, but they include user identifiers. can you accept anonymized traces or do you need schema changes?

[03:34] Alex Reed: anonymized traces are fine. we usually ask for: timestamp, endpoint id, request token count, response token count, and a short hashed prompt id so we can reconstitute distributions. no PII.

[03:44] Nina Alvarez: security question — what's your stance on KMS integration for private deployments? we need to keep keys in our KMS.

[03:50] Priya Nair: understood — for private and dedicated we support customer-managed KMS (AWSKMS and HSM integrations are supported). we'll include an audit log export in the POC deliverables. for hosted we can offer bring-your-own-key if in dedicated plan, otherwise we discuss additional compliance add-ons.

[04:06] Liam O'Connor: ok cool. next — success criteria. our product team wants SLOs that are measurable in the bench. i'm thinking: p99 latency target for short-turns under 350ms, 95th for medium-turns under 1s, and less than 1.5s for 99th of long responses. feasibility?

[04:25] Priya Nair: those are ambitious but achievable depending on model choice and instance type. short-turns under 350ms usually require a streaming-optimized model on NVLink-equipped GPUs or strong batching + prefix cache. for p99 on short-turns we often recommend a dedicated pool with KV cache warm-up. hosted API at lower TCO might hit 95th but pushing p99 < 350ms consistently across bursts is tougher.

[04:52] Samir Patel: when you say KV cache warm-up — how long is warm-up and how does that affect the first requests after a deploy?

[04:58] Priya Nair: warm-up depends on path length and the number of unique prompts, but in our tests you typically see warm-up effects fade in 10–30 minutes for steady prefixes; for cold-start you can pre-populate cache with representative prefixes ahead of the test. that's something we'll recommend in the runbook.

[05:19] Jordan Lee: also to quantify, we should capture tail-latency quantiles (p50, p90, p95, p99, p999) and token-level breakdowns: tokens/sec per GPU, average tokens per request.

[05:31] Alex Reed: can you remind us of the model family you're targeting? small-medium Llama-derivatives or larger instruction-tuned models?

[05:38] Samir Patel: we want to test a few models: an open medium model for cost baseline (like a 7B-type), and a higher-quality 13–30B variant for quality checks. we might also try a quantized 13B to see tradeoffs.

[05:50] Priya Nair: perfect. that gives a clear matrix: model sizes x quantization x deployment mode (hosted/dedicated) x workload shapes. we'll define measurable KPIs for latency, throughput, and quality (we'll use a small eval set for semantic fidelity).

[06:04] Maya Chen: can we also capture memory utilization per instance and KV cache hit rates? ops wants those metrics for capacity planning.

[06:11] Priya Nair: yes — we'll export GPU utilization, memory, nvlink stats, and cache hit rates. we also instrument per-token cost so you can see unit economics.

[06:21] Samir Patel: good. on timelines — what's realistic for the POC run and deliverables? our target is a 3-week pilot: week 0 prep and data handoff, week 1 bench runs, week 2 analysis and remediation, then decision.

[06:34] Alex Reed: that's tight but doable. our suggested timeline: 1 week for trace ingest + bench setup, 1 week for multiple run permutations (hosted vs dedicated, model variants), 1 week for deep analysis and final recommendations. so same roughly. we'll aim to have a bench plan in 4 business days.

[06:50] Liam O'Connor: what's the effort on Avalon side? how many engineers do you expect to be involved during bench windows?

[06:56] Priya Nair: usually an SRE to coordinate the trace and a single eng contact for clarifications needed — so 2 FTEs for the active week plus periodic check-ins. that's in line with what we saw from you.

[07:07] Alex Reed: quick note on cost modeling — we'll provide a simple cost calculator that combines tokens/sec, instance-hours, and model efficiency so you can compare hosted per-token vs dedicated monthly commit.

[07:20] Samir Patel: nice. one more item — quality gating. our product team won't accept a model that drops high-level intent in more than 2% of samples. how do you propose we measure that?

[07:29] Priya Nair: we typically run an automated eval on a subset of representative prompts (we call it the checkset) measuring intent-preservation and hallucination rate. we'll propose thresholds and manual spot-checking for borderline cases. put this as a success gate: intent-preservation >= 98% across the checkset.

[07:45] Jordan Lee: also we can do A/B diff quality checks between model variants and include a small human-in-the-loop labeling pass for ambiguous cases.

[07:54] Maya Chen: regarding deployment — Avalon prefers VPC peering and our own KMS. is it straightforward to test a dedicated cluster in our VPC for the POC?

[08:02] Priya Nair: yes, we can stand up a dedicated pool inside your VPC (private deployment) for the POC; timeline to provision depends on cloud account approvals — typically 2–4 business days after account info + infra access. if time is tight we can run initial tests on Redwood-hosted in the same region to validate the workload shape before private provisioning.

[08:20] Samir Patel: for logs and telemetry, we need the ability to stream audit logs into our SIEM — is that part of the POC?

[08:26] Alex Reed: absolutely — audit log export and a sample integration to your SIEM is standard for enterprise trials. we'll include that in the runbook.

[08:33] Liam O'Connor: ok what's the gating criteria to call the POC successful? summarizing what we've heard: latency SLOs met across quantiles, intent-preservation >=98% on checkset, cost per 1M tokens within target band, and secure deployment (VPC/KMS) validated. anything missing?

[08:48] Nina Alvarez: data residency. we need to ensure any transient logs for EU customers stay within EU. can we set region pinning for some traffic?

[08:55] Priya Nair: yes, routing policies with region pinning are supported. for the POC we can pin EU traffic to eu-west-instances and demonstrate failover.

[09:05] Samir Patel: sounds good. now to more detailed modeling: we want to understand concurrency-to-latency curves. can you share an example curve so we can calibrate expectations?

[09:13] Jordan Lee: sure. in our internal run with a 13B quantized model on a 4-GPU node we saw linear latency until concurrency ~18, then tail blow-up after concurrency of ~30. short-turn p99 stayed below 300ms up to concurrency 12. burst handling depends heavily on batching and prefix cache hit rates. we'll include sample plots in the bench plan.

[09:37] Samir Patel: do you simulate KV cache cold start and compute impact?

[09:40] Priya Nair: yes — one of the bench runs explicitly wipes the cache and runs a cold-start scenario then a steady-state run so you can quantify the delta.

[09:49] Alex Reed: let's talk token distribution collection — easiest is CSV with columns: timestamp iso, endpoint, input_tokens, output_tokens, request_duration_ms, prompt_hash. that will let us reconstruct histograms and replay.

[10:01] Maya Chen: we can generate that easily from our proxy logs. we'll anonymize prompt_text and map to prompt_hash.

[10:07] Liam O'Connor: are there any pitfalls you've seen when customers compress 72h into 6h? we worry about unrealistic burst density.

[10:13] Priya Nair: good point — we use Poisson-preserving compression (maintains intermittent bursts) and an optional campaign injection pattern to reproduce heavy tail bursts. we'll propose two replay modes: fidelity-preserving (scale timeline but keep relative spacing) and stress mode (compress diurnal peaks).

[10:31] Samir Patel: on the bench harness — will you replay requests with original user-agent headers? we sometimes route based on UA which affects routing logic.

[10:36] Jordan Lee: we can reproduce headers except for any PII. replicate UA, region, and headers necessary for routing decisions, yes.

[10:43] Maya Chen: scheduling — we need a maintenance window for the blast. are you flexible on run times? we prefer 02:00–06:00 UTC to minimize production impact.

[10:50] Alex Reed: yes we can align on that window. for the big 420 QPS blast we'll coordinate but we'll run it in your non-production environment if available; otherwise we'll do careful routing to avoid affecting customers.

[11:01] Samir Patel: any additional telemetry you need beyond token counts? we have latencies broken down by our proxy, backend, database calls, etc.

[11:07] Priya Nair: the more, the better — we'll map end-to-end latencies. separate network transit times vs compute times helps us isolate the model runtime contribution. include per-request DB calls if you have them.

[11:18] Alex Reed: quick note on model quality: we'll run n-gram and embedding-similarity checks and also a small human label batch of ~200 examples. that should give you confidence on intent gates.

[11:29] Nina Alvarez: security again — we need evidence of SOC2 controls and a data processing addendum. can you send your security packet?

[11:36] Alex Reed: yes — i'll share the security pack (SOC2, ISO, DPA) after the call. we'll also provide a checklist for KMS and VPC peering.

[11:44] Priya Nair: ok, to capture deliverables: bench plan (matrix + replay modes), proposed instance sizing and cost model, telemetry dashboard template, security checklist, and the test harness. we aim to deliver the plan by 2026-09-27.

[11:58] Samir Patel: sounds great. one practical question: when comparing hosted vs dedicated, how do you normalize cost since hosted is per-token and dedicated is instance-commit?

[12:06] Alex Reed: we'll compute total TCO for the projected traffic across a month's profile: monthly instance-hours * instance cost + token costs (if any) vs hosted per-token * estimated token volume. we'll show break-even curves at different QPS and sustained vs bursty patterns.

[12:21] Liam O'Connor: what's the minimal dataset we should give you to get started?

[12:25] Priya Nair: a sanitized 72h CSV with columns we mentioned, plus a 50–100 sample checkset for quality eval and the mapping of high-level route IDs. also list of PII constraints and region pin rules.

[12:36] Samir Patel: we'll get that to you by 2026-09-30.

[12:40] Alex Reed: excellent. quick recap of next steps — i'll email the benchmark matrix + benchmark harness instructions tomorrow, priya will propose sizing options, samir/maya will share artifacts by end of week. then we'll plan a hands-on test window during the first week post-ingest.

[12:56] Maya Chen: one more question — for the model variants you mentioned (7b vs 13–30b), do you have recommended quantization profiles that preserve throughput without big quality drops?

[13:04] Priya Nair: yes — for 13B we typically test 4-bit quantization with FP16 fallback for attention kernels; we also test 8-bit as a conservative option. we'll include a small quality delta table for each quant profile.

[13:16] Samir Patel: great. how will we know when to switch from hosted to dedicated if we like the results? do you have a migration plan?

[13:22] Alex Reed: migration is mostly a routing change and a datastore for model version pinning. we provide a migration checklist: traffic cutover strategy, pre-warm caches, validation run, and rollback plan. we'll include that if you move to dedicated.

[13:35] Liam O'Connor: last admin — what's the expected cost to run the POC itself? is there a trial credit?

[13:42] Alex Reed: most POCs are complementary within reason; if additional heavy infrastructure is needed (long multi-day runs on dedicated HW) we'll discuss a limited trial credit. we'll outline that in the bench plan.

[13:52] Jordan Lee: ok, any last concerns on the technical side?

[13:56] Nina Alvarez: just confirm logs retention during the POC and whether we can control retention window.

[14:02] Priya Nair: retention is configurable for the POC; we'll propose a short retention with export to your SIEM.

[14:09] Alex Reed: great. if there are no other questions we'll recap action items and wrap.

[14:14] Samir Patel: quick clarification — you mentioned measuring p999 earlier; do you recommend capturing that for all runs?

[14:20] Priya Nair: yes capture p999 but treat it as a diagnostic; p99 and p95 are our primary SLOs for user experience. p999 helps identify pathological tails.

[14:30] Alex Reed: recap of action items (live): alex will send bench plan by 2026-09-27; priya will propose sizing by 2026-09-29; avalon exports trace + checkset by 2026-09-30; may a confirm security checklist and peering details by 2026-10-01.

[14:48] Samir Patel: okay thanks everyone. we'll prioritize the trace export. looking forward to the bench plan.

[14:55] Alex Reed: thanks all. we'll follow up in email with next steps and a calendar invite for the first replay window.

[15:02] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript quality: automated captions intermittently mis-attributed speaker labels near crosstalk; some product names like "KV cache" transcribed as "k v cash" in places. preserved natural speech, fillers, and brief interrupts for realism.
